Tirzepatide may be the most powerful weight-loss drug yet. Unlike semaglutide, which targets GLP-1, tirzepatide activates both GLP-1 and GIP, two hormones involved in hunger, insulin, and metabolism. That dual approach produced remarkable results.

In major clinical trials, patients lost more than 20% of their body weight, with some studies pushing average losses even higher. Tirzepatide also outperformed semaglutide head-to-head and showed benefits for sleep apnea, liver disease, blood pressure, and diabetes risk.
But there are trade-offs. Some weight loss comes from lean muscle, the drug can cost hundreds or thousands of dollars per month, and weight often returns after treatment stops. High prices have also fueled a dangerous gray market where people buy raw tirzepatide powder online and mix injections themselves.

The drug works. Getting it safely is the harder part.

Why do people living in some of the hottest deserts on Earth wear MORE clothing instead of less? It seems completely backwards.

When temperatures climb above 110 °F, most people instinctively reach for shorts and a T-shirt. But in an extreme desert, exposing more skin can actually make the situation worse. Hot air hitting bare skin doesn’t always cool you. When the air is hotter than your body, it can transfer heat into you while accelerating sweat loss and dehydration. That’s why desert cultures such as the Bedouins developed loose, full-body clothing designed specifically for dry heat.
Traditional robes create a layer of air between the fabric and the skin, shielding the body from direct solar radiation while allowing hot air to rise and escape through the openings. As the wearer walks, the fabric moves and helps pump air through the garment, creating a natural ventilation system. Even black robes can work surprisingly well.
